questions.prompt: How does a switch statement in Swift differ from a switch statement in C or Java? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that Swift switch statements are exhaustive by default
Explains that Swift switch cases do not fall through automatically
Mentions support for advanced pattern matching such as intervals or where clauses

questions.modelAnswer: In Swift, switch statements are exhaustive, meaning all possible values must be handled or a default case must be supplied. Unlike C or Java, Swift switch cases do not fall through automatically, so developers do not need break statements to stop execution. Furthermore, Swift switch statements support rich pattern matching with intervals, tuples, and where clauses.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Control Flow

questions.prompt: What is the difference between while and repeat-while loops in Swift? When would you use each? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that while evaluates its condition at the start before executing the body
Explains that repeat-while evaluates its condition at the end, running at least once
Provides clear use cases for when an initial execution is guaranteed or required

questions.modelAnswer: A while loop evaluates its boolean condition at the start of each iteration, meaning its body might never run if the initial condition is false. In contrast, a repeat-while loop evaluates its condition at the end, guaranteeing the body executes at least once. You use repeat-while when an initial attempt is required, such as prompting user input before validating it.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Control Flow

questions.prompt: Why does Swift require the else block of a guard statement to transfer control? How does guard let differ from if let in variable scope? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that guard else must exit scope to prevent invalid execution
Explains that guard let keeps unwrapped variables bound in the outer scope
Contrasts with if let which scopes unwrapped variables only to its inner block

questions.modelAnswer: Swift requires the else block of a guard statement to transfer control out of scope. Using return, throw, or break makes sure execution stops if preconditions fail. Unlike if let, which scopes unwrapped variables only inside its curly braces, guard let keeps unwrapped variables available for the rest of the outer scope. This keeps the primary logic flat and avoids deep nesting.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Control Flow

questions.prompt: Explain how pattern matching with where clauses works in Swift switch statements. Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that where clauses add an extra boolean condition to a switch case
Notes that the case only matches if both the pattern and the where expression evaluate to true
Mentions that bound variables from the pattern can be used inside the where clause

questions.modelAnswer: A where clause in a switch statement allows developers to append an additional boolean check to a case pattern. The case only matches if the pattern matches and the where condition evaluates to true. Variables bound in the pattern can be inspected directly inside the where clause, allowing fine-grained checks such as verifying that two tuple coordinates are equal.

questions.prompt: What are labeled statements in Swift, and how do they resolve ambiguities when nesting multiple loops? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Defines labeled statements as naming a loop or control block with an identifier
Explains that break or continue can specify the label to target an outer loop
Highlights that this avoids awkward boolean flags when breaking out of nested loops

questions.modelAnswer: A labeled statement prefixes a loop or conditional block with a unique identifier followed by a colon. When loops are nested, a standard break or continue statement only affects the innermost loop. By writing break labelName or continue labelName, developers can target an outer loop directly, eliminating the need for complicated boolean flags.
